Assume Countable Choice for the Lebesgue-measure convention. A real-valued function $\sigma:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ belongs to the activation class $\mathcal M$ when it is Lebesgue measurable, is locally essentially bounded, and the closure of its discontinuity set has one-dimensional Lebesgue measure zero. Here locally essentially bounded means that for every compact interval $J\subset\mathbb R$ there is a finite $M_J$ such that $|\sigma(t)|\le M_J$ for Lebesgue-almost every $t\in J$. The discontinuity set is $\{t:\sigma\text{ is not continuous at }t\}$. The function is a polynomial almost everywhere when there is a real algebraic polynomial $p$ such that $\sigma=p$ outside a Lebesgue-null set.

The subclass $\mathcal M_{\mathrm{pt}}$ consists of those $\sigma\in\mathcal M$ that are also pointwise locally bounded: $\sup_{t\in J}|\sigma(t)|<\infty$ for every compact interval $J$. This extra condition distinguishes pointwise uniform approximation from approximation in the essential-supremum norm.

Let $d\ge1$ and let $\sigma:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be an activation function. For a finite width $m\in\mathbb N_0$, output weights $a_1,\ldots,a_m\in\mathbb R$, input weights $w_1,\ldots,w_m\in\mathbb R^d$, hidden biases $b_1,\ldots,b_m\in\mathbb R$, and output bias $c\in\mathbb R$, the scalar single-hidden-layer realization is

$$N(x)=c+\sum_{j=1}^{m}a_j\sigma(w_j\cdot x+b_j),\qquad x\in\mathbb R^d.$$

The family $\mathcal N_\sigma^{(d)}$ consists of all such functions as $m$ and the real parameters vary; $m=0$ is allowed and gives constant functions. This is the scalar-output, one-hidden-layer specialization of a layered multilayer perceptron with linear output.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\ge1$, let $K\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be compact, and let $\sigma\in\mathcal M_{\mathrm{pt}}$ not agree almost everywhere with any polynomial. Then the finite scalar single-hidden-layer networks with activation $\sigma$ are uniformly dense in $C(K,\mathbb R)$.

Let $\mu$ be a finite regular Borel measure on $\mathbb R^d$ concentrated on a compact set $K\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, and let $1\le p<\infty$. Form the real $L^p(\mu)$ space using the Borel $\sigma$-algebra. Then restrictions to $K$ of real-valued compactly supported continuous functions on $\mathbb R^d$ are dense in $L^p(\mu;\mathbb R)$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\ge1$, $w\in\mathbb R^d\setminus\{0\}$, $b\in\mathbb R$, and let $E\subseteq\mathbb R$ have Lebesgue outer measure zero. Then

$$\{x\in\mathbb R^d:w\cdot x+b\in E\}$$

is Lebesgue measurable and has $d$-dimensional Lebesgue measure zero. Consequently, if two Lebesgue measurable real functions on $\mathbb R$ agree outside a null set, their compositions with the same nonconstant affine form $x\mapsto w\cdot x+b$ agree almost everywhere on $\mathbb R^d$.

Assume Countable Choice. For every integer $d\ge1$, if

$$P(x_1,\ldots,x_d)=\sum_{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^d}c_\alpha x_1^{\alpha_1}\cdots x_d^{\alpha_d},$$

is a nonzero real polynomial with finitely many nonzero coefficients, then its zero set $\{x\in\mathbb R^d:P(x)=0\}$ is Lebesgue measurable and has $d$-dimensional Lebesgue measure zero.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\ge1$, $q\in\mathbb N_0$, and let $\sigma:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be measurable and equal almost everywhere to a polynomial of degree at most $q$ (including the zero polynomial). For every finite single-hidden-layer network with activation $\sigma$, its restriction to the segment $K=\{te_1:0\le t\le1\}\subset\mathbb R^d$ cannot approximate the target $f(te_1)=t^{q+1}$ uniformly with error less than

$$\varepsilon_q=\frac{(q+1)!}{2^{q+2}(q+1)^{q+1}}>0.$$

Consequently these networks are not uniformly dense in $C(K,\mathbb R)$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $p$ be a real number with
$0<p<\infty$. Write $\mathcal M(X,\mu)$ for the measurable functions
$f:X\to\mathbb R$. For $f\in\mathcal M(X,\mu)$ define the extended-valued
$p$-functional

$$\|f\|_p:=\begin{cases}\left(\int |f|^p\,d\mu\right)^{1/p},&\displaystyle\int |f|^p\,d\mu<\infty,\\+\infty,&\displaystyle\int |f|^p\,d\mu=+\infty.\end{cases}$$

The finite power uses [[def-real-power]], while the second clause avoids
applying real powers to the extended value $+\infty$. The integral is the
nonnegative Lebesgue integral of [[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]].

The class

$$\mathcal L^p(\mu):=\{f\in\mathcal M(X,\mu): \|f\|_p<\infty\}$$

is the measurable-function space used on this page before passing to
almost-everywhere equivalence classes.

For $1\le p<\infty$, the pointwise operations make $\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ a real
vector space by
[[thm-calligraphic-l-p-and-l-infinity-are-vector-spaces-for-p-at-least-one]].

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

- For $0<p<\infty$, define an equivalence relation on $\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ by
  $$f\sim g\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f-g\in\mathcal N(\mu),$$
  and write $L^p(\mu)$ for the set of classes $[f]$.
- For $p=\infty$, define the same relation on $L^\infty(\mu)$ and again write
  $L^\infty(\mu)$ for the set of classes.

Thus an element of $L^p(\mu)$ is an almost-everywhere equivalence class of
measurable representatives.

When $1\le p\le\infty$, the displayed set quotient agrees with the usual
quotient-vector-space construction of
[[def-quotient-vector-space-and-canonical-projection]].

For $0<p<1$, the same class notation is used; under its stated choice hypothesis, the later item
[[thm-the-l-p-distance-for-zero-less-p-less-one-is-a-complete-translation-invariant-metric]]
supplies the metric structure rather than a normed-space structure.

Let $\mu$ be a positive measure and let $
u$ be a signed measure or a complex measure on the same measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$. We say that $
u$ is **absolutely continuous with respect to $\mu$**, and write
$$
u\ll\mu,$$
if every measurable $\mu$-null set is also $
u$-null:
$$\mu(E)=0\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad 
u(E)=0\qquad(E\in\mathcal A).$$
Because every measurable subset of a $\mu$-null set is again $\mu$-null, this is equivalent to requiring $
u(F)=0$ for every measurable $F\subseteq E$ whenever $\mu(E)=0$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $X$ be a set and let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on $X$ ([[def-sigma-algebra]]). A **measure** on $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a function

$$\mu:\mathcal A\longrightarrow[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$$

such that:

1. $\mu(\varnothing)=0$;
2. for every pairwise disjoint sequence $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$,
   $$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k),$$
   where the right side is the nonnegative extended sum of [[def-nonnegative-extended-series]].

The second condition is **countable additivity**. It begins at index $0$ and includes the case in which some term or the total sum is $+\infty$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: If $\sigma\in\mathcal M_{\mathrm{pt}}$ is nonpolynomial almost everywhere, [F3] proves pointwise uniform density on every compact $K$. If $\sigma$ is polynomial almost everywhere, [F7] gives a specific compact segment on which density fails.

Now let $\sigma\in\mathcal M$ and put $C=\overline{D_\sigma}$, its closed null discontinuity set. Definition [F1] supplies the local essential bound and null-closure hypotheses. Define $\widetilde\sigma=\sigma$ off $C$ and $\widetilde\sigma=0$ on $C$. This is measurable and equals $\sigma$ almost everywhere. For a compact interval $J$, choose a larger compact interval $J'$ containing $J$ in its interior and an essential bound $M_{J'}$ for $\sigma$ there. At any $t\in J\setminus C$, continuity of $\sigma$ implies $|\sigma(t)|\le M_{J'}$: a strict violation would, by continuity, give an interval of positive measure inside $J'$ on which $|\sigma|>M_{J'}$. Thus $\widetilde\sigma$ is pointwise locally bounded; outside $C$ it is continuous, so the closure of its discontinuities is contained in $C$. It belongs to $\mathcal M_{\mathrm{pt}}$; if $\sigma$ is nonpolynomial almost everywhere, so is $\widetilde\sigma$.

For the converse, suppose $\sigma=p_0$ almost everywhere for a polynomial $p_0$ of degree $q$. By [F5] and [F8], every nonconstant unit equals $p_0(w_j\cdot x+b_j)$ for $\mu$-almost every $x$; constant-input units can be absorbed into the output bias. Hence every network represents, in $L^p(\mu)$, a polynomial of total degree at most $q$.

For any finite $\widetilde\sigma$-network, a unit with $w_j\ne0$ differs from the corresponding $\sigma$-unit only on the null pullback $\{x:w_j\cdot x+b_j\in C\}$, null by [F5]. Replace the output bias by $c+\sum_{w_j=0}a_j(\widetilde\sigma(b_j)-\sigma(b_j))$ to absorb the constant-input units. The resulting $\sigma$-network equals the $\widetilde\sigma$-network almost everywhere in $\mathbb R^d$, and hence defines the same Borel $L^p(\mu)$ class under the representative convention when $\mu\ll\lambda_d$. For nonpolynomial-almost-everywhere $\sigma$, applying [F3] to $\widetilde\sigma$ and transferring these approximants proves essential-supremum density for $\mathcal M$ on every compact $K$.

Assume $\mu(K)>0$ and let $P_q$ be the vector space of real polynomials in $d$ variables of total degree at most $q$. In a monomial basis its coefficient space is finite dimensional. The map $P\mapsto\|P\|_{L^p(\mu)}$ is continuous in the coefficients because $K$ is compact and $\mu$ is finite. It is strictly positive on every nonzero coefficient vector: by [F6] its zero set is Lebesgue null, hence $\mu$-null by [F8], while $\mu(K)>0$. The coefficient unit sphere is closed and bounded, hence compact by [F9]; the norm map has a positive minimum $a$ there, so $\|P\|_{L^p(\mu)}\ge a|\operatorname{coeff}(P)|$. Any $L^p$-Cauchy sequence in $P_q$ has Cauchy coefficients and converges to a polynomial in $P_q$, so $P_q$ is closed in $L^p(\mu)$.

To justify the Borel convention, $C$ is closed, $\widetilde\sigma=0$ on $C$, and $\widetilde\sigma$ is continuous on the open complement of $C$, so $\widetilde\sigma$ is Borel measurable. For any raw $\sigma$-network $N$, replace only its nonconstant units by $\widetilde\sigma$-units and keep each constant-input value $a_j\sigma(b_j)$ in the output bias. The resulting Borel function $N^*$ is bounded on $K$ by pointwise local boundedness of $\widetilde\sigma$ and compactness of each affine image. It equals $N$ outside the finite union of the closed Lebesgue-null sets $\{x:w_j\cdot x+b_j\in C\}$ with $w_j\ne0$, by [F5]. Hence $N^*$ lies in $L^p(\mu)$. Any two Borel representatives of $N$ agreeing with it Lebesgue-almost everywhere differ on a Borel Lebesgue-null set, which is $\mu$-null by [F8], so they define the same class. This also justifies the polynomial representatives in step 1.3 and the transfers in step 2.1 without assuming raw networks are Borel measurable.

The polynomial $r(x)=x_1^{q+1}$ is not in $P_q$ modulo $\mu$-almost-everywhere equality: for every $P\in P_q$, $r-P$ is a nonzero polynomial, so [F6]–[F8] imply $\mu(\{x\in K:r(x)=P(x)\})=0<\mu(K)$. Thus the closed subspace $P_q$ is proper and cannot be dense. Step 1.3 places the whole network family inside it, proving failure of $L^p$ density for polynomial-almost-everywhere activations.

Suppose $\mu(K)>0$. By [F10], $\mu$ is a measure, and the real Borel $L^p$ convention is fixed in the Statement. To prove the positive $L^p$ sufficiency, choose any real class $[f]\in L^p(\mu;\mathbb R)$ and $\varepsilon>0$. By [F4], choose $u\in C_c(\mathbb R^d,\mathbb R)$ with $\|f-u\|_{L^p(\mu)}<\varepsilon/2$. Apply [F3] to $\widetilde\sigma$ on $K$ to choose a network $N_{\widetilde\sigma}$ with $\sup_{x\in K}|N_{\widetilde\sigma}(x)-u(x)|<\varepsilon/(2\mu(K)^{1/p})$. By step 2.1 replace it by a $\sigma$-network equal $\mu$-almost everywhere. Using the Borel representative supplied by steps 2.1 and 3.1, $\|N-u\|_{L^p(\mu)}=\|N_{\widetilde\sigma}-u\|_{L^p(\mu)}\le\mu(K)^{1/p}\sup_K|N_{\widetilde\sigma}-u|$. The triangle inequality yields $\|N-f\|_{L^p(\mu)}<\varepsilon$.

If $\mu=0$, every measurable real function represents the zero class in $L^p(\mu;\mathbb R)$, and the network family contains zero by width zero and output bias zero. Thus it is dense regardless of $\sigma$. Together with steps 4.1 and 3.2, this proves the stated $L^p$ equivalence and its zero-measure boundary.

Finally take $\mu$ to be Lebesgue measure restricted to $[0,1]^d$. If a polynomial-almost-everywhere activation gave essential-supremum approximation to every continuous target there, the estimate $\|N-f\|_{L^p(\mu)}\le\|N-f\|_{L^\infty(\mu)}$ would contradict step 3.2 for $f(x)=x_1^{q+1}$. This proves the essential-supremum obstruction on the cube and completes both compact-set equivalences.

Assume Countable Choice for the Lebesgue-measure convention. A real-valued function $\sigma:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ belongs to the activation class $\mathcal M$ when it is Lebesgue measurable, is locally essentially bounded, and the closure of its discontinuity set has one-dimensional Lebesgue measure zero. Here locally essentially bounded means that for every compact interval $J\subset\mathbb R$ there is a finite $M_J$ such that $|\sigma(t)|\le M_J$ for Lebesgue-almost every $t\in J$. The discontinuity set is $\{t:\sigma\text{ is not continuous at }t\}$. The function is a polynomial almost everywhere when there is a real algebraic polynomial $p$ such that $\sigma=p$ outside a Lebesgue-null set.

The subclass $\mathcal M_{\mathrm{pt}}$ consists of those $\sigma\in\mathcal M$ that are also pointwise locally bounded: $\sup_{t\in J}|\sigma(t)|<\infty$ for every compact interval $J$. This extra condition distinguishes pointwise uniform approximation from approximation in the essential-supremum norm.

Assume Countable Choice. Fix $d\ge1$ and use the finite scalar single-hidden-layer family

$$\mathcal N_\sigma^{(d)}=\left\{x\mapsto c+\sum_{j=1}^m a_j\sigma(w_j\cdot x+b_j):m\in\mathbb N_0,\ c,a_j,b_j\in\mathbb R,\ w_j\in\mathbb R^d\right\}.$$

For every compact $K\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, if $\sigma\in\mathcal M_{\mathrm{pt}}$ is not equal almost everywhere to a polynomial, then $\mathcal N_\sigma^{(d)}$ is uniformly dense in $C(K,\mathbb R)$. More generally, if $\sigma\in\mathcal M$ is not polynomial almost everywhere, this family is dense for the essential-supremum seminorm on each such $K$ with respect to $d$-dimensional Lebesgue measure. If instead $\sigma$ agrees almost everywhere with a polynomial of degree at most $q$ for some $q\in\mathbb N_0$ (including the zero polynomial), the family is not uniformly dense on the segment $\{te_1:0\le t\le1\}$, and is not dense in the Lebesgue essential-supremum seminorm on $[0,1]^d$. Thus pointwise compact-uniform density for $\mathcal M_{\mathrm{pt}}$, and essential-supremum density for $\mathcal M$, each hold on every compact set if and only if $\sigma$ is not polynomial almost everywhere.

Let $1<p<\infty$, and let $\mu$ be a finite regular Borel measure concentrated on a compact $K\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ and absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure. Form the real $L^p(\mu)$ space using the Borel $\sigma$-algebra. For $\sigma\in\mathcal M$, a network is interpreted in this space through any Borel representative agreeing with it outside a Lebesgue-null set; these representatives exist, are integrable on $K$, and give a unique $L^p(\mu)$ class. This convention does not alter the actual pointwise network used in the uniform clause. For $\sigma\in\mathcal M$ and $\mu(\mathbb R^d)>0$, $\mathcal N_\sigma^{(d)}$ is dense in $L^p(\mu;\mathbb R)$ if and only if $\sigma$ is not polynomial almost everywhere. If $\mu=0$, then $L^p(\mu;\mathbb R)=\{0\}$ and the network family is dense for every $\sigma\in\mathcal M$, including polynomial activations.

These are existence statements without a quantitative width bound. They imply neither trainability nor statistical generalization, and compact-uniform approximation does not mean uniform approximation on all of $\mathbb R^d$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: ReLU and logistic sigmoid are continuous, hence their discontinuity sets are empty; ReLU is bounded on each compact interval and sigmoid is globally bounded between zero and one. Thus both lie in the pointwise locally bounded activation class.

Neither is a polynomial almost everywhere. If a continuous function equals a polynomial almost everywhere on $\mathbb R$, their difference is continuous and must vanish everywhere, since any nonzero value would persist on an open interval of positive measure. ReLU vanishes on $(-\infty,0)$ but is positive on $(0,\infty)$; the sigmoid is bounded and nonconstant. These properties exclude a polynomial identity for each.

Applying the pointwise $\mathcal M_{\mathrm{pt}}$ branch of [F2] separately to each activation proves the stated compact-uniform approximation property. Both activations and their networks are continuous, so they are already Borel representatives when the theorem's $L^p$ clause is used. The theorem is an existence statement only and supplies no uniform width bound.
